newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Waiting for the Q4 ECI.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Waiting for the Q4 ECI.

text.p: With no fresh economic data on tap, the market could spend Friday waiting for the Employment Cost Index (ECI), a fourth-quarter gauge not due until Tuesday and watching the dollar's performance in the foreign exchange markets, strategists and analysts said.

"Waiting for the ECI is the most important factor going forward because everyone is very concerned about what's going on on the wage inflation front," Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.

"In the market's mind, the ECI has the potential to determine whether the Federal Reserve will raise rates in this quarter or not," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets.
In Friday's vacuum of economic data, the movements of the dollar in the foreign exchange markets could help guide prices of U.S. government securities, some participants said.

"The odds favor a quiet Friday, but in a data vacuum, the major influence on Treasury trading is how the dollar fares on world foreign exchange markets," said William Sullivan, senior vice president at Dean Witter Reynolds.
"Any significant appreciation by the dollar will be greeted warmly by the Treasury market," said Sullian.
The dollar hit a 47-month high against the yen in foreign exchange trading in New York on Thursday.
Alexy, however, was more skeptical of the dollar's influence on government securities trading.
"A high dollar doesn't necessarily bring in buyers of Treasuries," he said. "A dollar that is going higher brings in buyers."

Alexy said "the big question mark" is whether central banks will intervene to damp the dollar's rise "or whether 120 (versus the yen) is an objective that will be reached, glanced at and quickly surpassed on the way to something else."
Once that question is resolved, "you'll see currency related participation in the Treasury market."
Traders said the market will also be working on distributing new supply, traders said.
The Treasury sold $17.5 billion in two-year notes on Wednesday and $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Thursday.

Sullivan said "there's a sense" that the auctions were heavily subscribed to by dealers. Alexy said "some speculative accounts" probably bought at the auction and the market was "unlikely to run too much before the ECI number prints."

That the market traded lower at the results of each auction on Wednesday and on Thursday indicates that "people have given up on the upside prospects of the market," said Karydakis. "We need news to break us out -- like the ECI."
The 30-year benchmark Treasury bond was trading at 95-15/32, down 9/32 and yielding 6.86 percent, in late afternoon trade on Thursday.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open between 5-1/8 and 5-3/16 percent on Friday.
